title: A powerful solar flare
values: X8.7 flare; peak 12:51 p.m. EDT (16:51 UTC)
note: Solar observation, not a Mars surface dose. Our scenario separately models protection and exposure. DONKI network retrieval was unavailable; this verified SDO archive is the offline historical trigger.

title: Continued solar activity
values: SDO recorded continuing X-class activity; nine X-class flares during May 10–16.
note: An alternative historical trigger. Modeled colony exposure is not inferred directly from flare class.

title: Sunlight lost to Martian dust
dataset: 2018 global dust storm, JPL recovery archive
note: Larger optical depth means less sunlight. The game's 18–35% solar yield and 3-sol storm are balancing assumptions, not a reproduction of Opportunity's energy curve.

title: Weather at Jezero Crater
dataset: First MEDA weather report; archived NASA report
note: Archived extrema inform the modeled temperature cycle and extra heating demand. The game does not stream calibrated MEDA time-series products. The PDS archive is linked separately.

title: MEDA science archive
values: Air temperature, pressure, humidity, wind, radiation and dust sensors
note: MEDA's Radiation and Dust Sensor measures optical radiation and dust, not astronaut ionizing dose. Use Curiosity RAD for the ionizing-radiation teaching reference.

title: Radiation measured on Mars
values: Average dose equivalent: 0.67 mSv per Earth day in this observation interval
note: A location- and time-specific historical average, not today's Mars-wide rate. Multiplied by 24.6597/24 for the illustrative per-sol metric. It never directly changes health scores.

title: Planning breathable air
values: Nominal metabolic oxygen planning value: 0.84 kg per person per Earth day
note: Converted to 0.863 kg/person/sol using 24.6597/24. Activity, diet and individual physiology vary; this is a simplified planning model.

title: Messages take time
values: Earth-to-Mars one-way radio delay: approximately 3–22 minutes
note: The scenario chooses a one-way delay within that range. Waiting uses a fractional sol for a round-trip plus 60 minutes of planning, not an entire sol of signal travel.

title: Why space biology needs careful interpretation
dataset: Mouse muscle and bone research across spaceflight studies
observed: Archived study; about 30 days of spaceflight
values: Mouse tissue research examines GSK3 and muscle/bone responses; it is not a human survival calculator.
note: Used only for qualitative educational context about living systems and research. No mouse outcome is converted to human health loss or mortality probability.

title: How long does the journey take?
instrument: NASA Kennedy Space Center / Mars mission engineering
dataset: Rocket Ranch, Episode 1: Mars; mission planning reference
values: Typical Earth-to-Mars travel: six to nine months one way, roughly 0.5–0.75 Earth years.
note: Trajectory, departure window and propulsion affect transit time. This cinematic chooses 210 Earth days (about seven months or 0.57 years) and compresses them into 60 seconds. Its path, planet spacing, booster sequence and landing are illustrations, not orbital flight predictions. A round-trip mission also needs a surface stay and return flight.
